title: No mixed bands: playing only with white bands until the Washingtonians
summary: Greer says there were no mixed bands, that he never played a gig with a Black band before the Washingtonians, and credits Benny Goodman with presenting integrated groups.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What I wanted to do, was it unusual when you were working the band with the white guys when you were a teenager, was that considered unusual or were there many mixed bands.
That's the only one, the one you were with.

I never in my life played with a colored band on a gig. Of course, I belonged to the Clef Club and I rehearsed with them, but on an actual gig, I never in my life played with no colored band till we had the Washingtonians.

I never took it, never concentrate on it that serious, because I never come in contact with it that much, as far as playing was concerned. I knew that the colored musicians, we had just millions of them, fabulous, could play in Harlem. You could go right next door and hear the damndest horn blowing things you ever heard in your life, drummers, Big Sid Catlett, all them guys, Jabbo on trumpet, sure, Sidney DeParis and all them guys, sharks, because they had to be because it was a jungle. Everybody waiting for you to make a mistake and they got you, but didn't have no colored playing with white-black like now.
I think Benny Goodman was the first one to present them to the public when he had Teddy and Hamp-- Lionel, in his quartet, Gene.
